title: Texas Hog Monitoring Checklist for Landowners
content:
TL;DR: Use this Texas hog monitoring checklist to assign each trap an owner, confirm camera health, count the complete sounder, and decide whether a field visit is necessary. Remote footage supports trap timing and movement records; it does not replace livestock checks or agency reporting.

A trap site can look quiet at daylight and still be busy all night. A Texas hog monitoring checklist gives the team one way to see that activity, decide when to drive, and know who can close the gate when the full sounder commits. The result is fewer empty trips and better capture decisions.

Remote monitoring also closes a visibility gap between routine livestock checks and the wildlife routes that cross a property after dark. It cannot diagnose screwworm or replace hands-on animal checks. If you suspect a case, contact USDA APHIS and your state agricultural extension office. Use the camera for movement evidence and trap operations, not a medical conclusion.

Give Every Site an Owner

Start with names, not equipment. Assign one person to review active feeds each day and a backup who can send a closure command. The same person should not have to remember every site detail. Keep a short log with the site name, estimated sounder size, last bait change, nights of activity, and catch result.

Map the primary baited trap, any secondary crossing, and the water or fence line that keeps pulling hogs away. Label each camera and gate the same way in the app and field.

Make the Daily Review Answer Three Questions

  1. Is the camera healthy? Confirm power, cell reporting, and a readable day and night view.
  2. Is the sounder ready? Count the group and note which hogs still stop at the edge.
  3. Does the site need a drive? Look for flooding, empty bait, gate trouble, a moved mount, or another problem that cannot be solved remotely.

A live wild hog trap camera system turns that review into an operating decision. The HogEye Steel Camera is built for trap-site use and live closure control. A landowner can check the site from the truck or office, then save the drive for work that actually needs boots on the ground.

Know What the Picture Is Telling You

A blank feed and a quiet site are not the same thing. Loss of power, a shifted mount, weak reporting, or vegetation across the lens can hide activity. Fix the view before changing the trapping plan.

When hogs circle the outside edge, keep conditioning. An early closure catches the bold animals and teaches the rest. When the complete sounder enters, settles, and feeds without watching the gate, the team has evidence for a clean drop. After the catch, keep the camera active long enough to see whether another sounder moves into the same route.

Install for the Decision You Need to Make

  • Frame the entrance, trap interior, and approach lane in one useful view.
  • Test day and night visibility from the final mount, not from the road.
  • Protect the camera from hog traffic, livestock, gate swing, and weather.
  • Test the closure command before the catch phase begins.
  • Confirm the selected AT&T or Verizon connection reports reliably at that site.

Keep Observation and Reporting in Their Lanes

Camera footage can show where feral hogs and other wildlife move. It can document a date, location, group size, and change in activity. It cannot confirm larvae, diagnose an animal, or recommend treatment. During a screwworm alert, keep agency contacts beside the trap log so a concern moves quickly to USDA APHIS and Texas extension instead of turning into speculation in a team text.

Run a Monthly Coverage Audit

Once a month, review the system instead of only the latest pictures. Confirm that every active trap reports, each feed has an owner, catches and sounder estimates are logged, and hot crossings have enough coverage. Fix ownership and uptime before adding another camera. Better discipline usually improves results faster than more hardware.

Frequently Asked Questions

What belongs on a Texas hog monitoring checklist?

Site ownership, camera health, sounder counts, bait and gate condition, closure authority, catch results, and current reporting contacts.

Can remote monitoring replace cattle checks?

No. It adds visibility on feral hog lines and wildlife crossings while livestock checks continue separately.

How often should an active trap be reviewed?

Review active feeds daily, update the sounder log when the pattern changes, and audit the full system monthly.

Turn the Checklist Into a Habit

The value of remote monitoring is not another screen. It is a team that knows what happened last night and what to do next. Give every trap an owner, protect the view, wait for the full sounder, and use field visits where they matter most.
